title: ICJ Set to Rule on Rohingya Genocide Case Against Myanmar: Global Stakes Unveiled
body:
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) will deliver its long‑awaited judgment next week on whether Myanmar bears responsibility for genocide against the Rohingya, a case lodged by The Gambia in 2019. The decision, the first genocide ruling by the United Nations’ principal judicial organ in more than a decade, could reshape diplomatic pressure on the Southeast Asian nation, affect ongoing sanctions, and set a legal precedent for how the world addresses mass atrocities against minority groups.

The Gambia’s filing, submitted on behalf of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, alleges that Myanmar’s military campaigns in Rakhine State since 2017 amount to a deliberate attempt to destroy the Rohingya, a Muslim minority denied citizenship under the 1982 nationality law. The complaint cites evidence of mass killings, sexual violence, forced displacement and the systematic burning of villages. Myanmar, which denies the accusations, argues that the actions constitute counter‑insurgency operations against armed Rohingya militants and that the case is politically motivated.

Legal scholars note that the ICJ’s jurisdiction hinges on the 1948 Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide, to which both Myanmar and The Gambia are parties. If the court finds that the requisite intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a protected group existed, it can order provisional measures, including the cessation of military operations, the protection of displaced populations, and the provision of reparations. While the ICJ cannot impose criminal penalties directly, its rulings carry significant moral and diplomatic weight, often prompting United Nations bodies and individual states to act.

The stakes extend beyond the immediate parties. Regional actors, particularly members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), have been reluctant to intervene in what they view as an internal matter. A genocide finding could force ASEAN to reconsider its principle of non‑interference, potentially leading to collective action or at least a unified condemnation. Moreover, the verdict may influence the International Criminal Court’s ongoing investigations into alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Myanmar, providing a judicial anchor for future prosecutions.

Humanitarian groups warn that the timing of the decision is critical. More than 800,000 Rohingya remain in camps in Bangladesh, while thousands are still trapped in Rakhine under a fragile ceasefire. A decisive ICJ ruling could accelerate the repatriation process, bolster calls for safe and voluntary returns, and pressure Myanmar’s military junta to grant citizenship and basic rights. Conversely, a narrow finding or a dismissal could embolden the regime, undermining decades of advocacy and leaving the Rohingya’s plight in a legal limbo.

The world will watch closely as the judges deliberate. Regardless of the outcome, the case underscores the growing expectation that international law can hold sovereign states accountable for mass atrocities. The forthcoming judgment will not only determine the legal label applied to Myanmar’s actions but also signal how the global community will respond when the threshold of genocide is alleged. As the ICJ prepares its verdict, diplomats, activists, and survivors alike hope that justice—however limited—will finally translate into tangible protection for a people long denied a voice.
